lines: The cat on the blue wall has not moved since lunch. Respect.
Biscuit walked past and inspected my shoes. I passed.
A gull is standing on the fountain like he owns it. Maybe he does.
Three o'clock. Even the cypresses look relaxed.
Somebody is practising the accordion upstairs. Getting better.
I have a book in my pocket. It has been there for three walks.
Odile told me a word for the crossword. I forgot it. Lovely word.
The gulls are taking turns on the lamp post. Very fair system.
A slow afternoon. My favourite speed.
Biscuit has decided I am allowed on the promenade. Takk, Biscuit.
Henri's radio is playing something old and cheerful. Perfect.
Half the town is on a bench. The other half is looking for one.
The cat blinked at me. I think that was a hello.
I walk the same route every afternoon. It is never the same walk.
Note to self: learn one more French word today. Maybe citron.
Afternoon plan: walk, coffee, think. In that order. Roughly.
Someone left a crossword on the bench. Two answers in. Tempting.
A gull just stole a crumb from another gull. Very polite about it.
Ha det, desk. Back in an hour. Probably two.
The string lights are off, resting up for tonight.
The palms are swaying in time with the café radio. Almost.
Léo just told me gulls have favourite colours. I am researching.
Kos. There is no English word. This afternoon is the word.
That cat has three walls and chooses the sunny one. Wise.
I counted the cypresses once. Then Léo counted them better.
Biscuit's tail goes faster near the café. Interesting data.
The fountain is in its afternoon mood. Slow and sparkly.
Somebody is whistling the song from last night. Catchy one.
Afternoons here are long in the nicest way.
Théo is reading a menu like it is a novel. Fair enough.
A gull on the kiosk roof is keeping watch. Over what, unclear.
New hobby: knowing which bench gets the sun at four.
The workbench has more neat little piles than yesterday.
He has labelled the screw drawers. By size. Then by mood.
I bring the coffee. He brings the progress. Fair trade.
Through the window I see one lamp, one plan, one happy man.
A new shelf in the workshop. It already has things on it.
I tap the glass. He holds up a tiny part. We both nod.
His tea has gone cold beside the vice. Sign of a good day.
The cat from the wall sometimes naps on his windowsill.
Small tidy steps in there. My favourite kind of progress.
He drew me a diagram on a napkin. I am keeping it.
The workshop clock is five minutes fast. On purpose, he says.
Pencil shavings on the floor. A crossword on the bench. Busy.
Twelve screwdrivers on the wall, in order. Very soothing.
I came to look in. I have been looking in for half an hour.
A gull is watching the workshop too. We are both curious.
He fixed the door hinge. It no longer sings. I miss it a bit.
Afternoon light through the workshop window. Like a painting.
He showed me a new clamp. It is a very good clamp.
One lap. Then maybe one more, for the sea.
Past the café, past the fountain, past the cat. Hei, cat.
Walking the promenade with my hands behind my back. Like Henri.
Biscuit and I walked the same stretch. He was faster.
This is where the ideas come. Somewhere near the third palm.
I say hei to everyone. Most of them say bonjour. Nice trade.
The gulls follow the stroll route too. Probably for the crumbs.
Halfway along, the sea goes from blue to bluer.
A walk is just thinking with better scenery.
Camille waved. Léo waved twice. That is the Léo rate.
Strolling. Not walking. Strolling has no destination.
I hum on these walks. Badly. The gulls do not mind.
Odile has a nod for every bench. I am learning them.
Past the string lights, past the planters. Lemons, still smug.
Lucie rang her bell at me. I rang an imaginary one back.
One loop of the promenade is exactly one good thought.
The cat came down off the wall to walk beside me. Briefly.
Someone is playing guitar by the fountain. I slowed down.
The walk back always looks different. Same palms, new light.
A gull landed on the railing and walked with me a while.
I left the phone at home. The promenade did not notice.
Kiosk coffee, small, black. Best four minutes of the afternoon.
The kiosk has a new postcard of the fountain. I bought two.
A coffee and the crossword page. Nothing else required.
The kiosk radio is playing a chanson. I almost know the words.
Biscuit waits by the kiosk. He knows where the biscuits are.
There is a gull who visits the kiosk at five. Punctual bird.
Kiosk stop. I stand, sip and watch the promenade go by.
Five down: a small shop that sells coffee. Kiosk. Too easy.
The cat has found the kiosk awning. Shade and a view.
Same cup, same corner, same view. Still not bored.
Lucie stopped for a coffee too. We clinked paper cups.
The kiosk sells a paper I cannot read. I buy it for the puzzles.
A coffee before golden hour. Getting ready for the good bit.
The kiosk lady saves me the last almond biscuit. Every time.
Two gulls and a cat, all ignoring each other beautifully.
Brought the builder a pastry. He set it down like a precious part.
The radio is on low. He knows all the words. Quietly.
A new shelf since yesterday. Very level. I checked twice.
Sawdust in the sunbeam. Like indoor snow, but warm.
He handed me a screw to hold. I am holding it with pride.
The door is propped open. The breeze comes in to help.
I said the bench looked tidy. He tidied it again, smiling.
Leaning on the doorframe. Best seat in the workshop.
He hums when a thing fits. Two hums so far this visit.
Somebody swept the step. Him, I suspect. Around noon.
I only came to wave. Now I know how a vise works.
Afternoon sun across the workbench. Everything looks finished.
A pencil behind his ear, a tidy bench. All is well.
Good joint, that. I know nothing about joints. Still good.
He offered me the good stool. I insisted he keep it.
Through the window he gave me a thumbs up. I gave two.
Pine and coffee in here. I will stay one more minute.
He fixed Léo's bike bell this morning. It rings in tune now.
I knock on the frame. He knocks back on the bench. Hei.
Two screwdrivers, both his favourite. Fair enough.
Warm stones underfoot. The promenade has had a sunny day.
A soft breeze off the water. Exactly the right amount.
Henri waved his watering can at me. I waved my hand back.
One slow lap. The palms are doing their rustling thing.
Odile liked my shirt. I will wear it again tomorrow.
Odile dropped her scarf. I got a whole thank-you speech.
Cypresses smell lovely in the warmth. Nobody warned me.
My thoughts usually catch up with me by the fountain.
Held the gate for Lucie and her bike. She rang a thank you.
The fountain is splashing the bench. The bench seems fine.
The breeze smells of lemons today. Henri's doing, probably.
Lap two. Léo says I walk like a man with a plan.
Walking slowly enough to read every shop sign. Twice.
The light is softer now. Even the zinc roofs look kind.
A visitor asked where the sea was. I pointed. We both smiled.
Sun on my neck, sea on my left. A good arrangement.
Somebody painted the railing this week. Very blue. Very nice.
I let a pigeon go first. He seemed to expect it.
Halfway round. Time to think about nothing in particular.
Camille said hei to me. She has been practising.
Théo is walking very slowly too. We nod like colleagues.
Warm afternoon. Even the gulls are strolling.
Henri gave me a lemon for the walk. I am carrying it carefully.
The shade under the palms moves a little each lap.
The whitewash is glowing. Someone should paint this. Maybe me.
A slow lap. The kind where you remember to look up.
Léo overtook me twice. I let him win both times.
Odile's bench gets the best breeze. She chose well, years ago.
Two coffees, please. One for whoever comes by next.
My cup has a little lemon painted on it. Lucky cup.
Paid for Henri's coffee. He will pretend not to notice.
Iced coffee, because the sun asked nicely.
Bought a postcard of this exact view. For my mother.
The kiosk has a new biscuit. I have been asked to report back.
Takk. Change in the jar, as always.
Lucie recommended the almond one. Lucie is never wrong.
Coffee, shade, a breeze. The kiosk understands me.
Both hands round the cup. Norwegian habit, even in the sun.
The kiosk umbrella is doing great work today.
They had my coffee ready before I asked. Small town, big heart.
Two sugar cubes. One for the coffee, one for later.
The afternoon is in no hurry. I am trying to match it.
Up north the sun would be getting shy by now. Here it stays.
Sun on the whitewash. Slightly too bright. Lovely.
Odile says I have kind ears. I am taking it.
Henri lent me his hat for the walk. Very French on me.
The breeze just tidied my hair for me. Thanks, breeze.
Lemon trees, sea air, a warm wall to lean on. Good afternoon.
Marcel waved a napkin at me from the terrace. I waved back.
Léo showed me a shell. I said it was excellent. It was.
I said thank you to the town. It did not answer. It glowed.
The cypresses stand so straight. I stand a bit straighter too.
Helped Henri carry a full watering can. He was very gracious.
Afternoons like this, I forget to check the time.
The fountain is the only one working hard today.
Every window open. Half the town is humming the same song.
Camille brought me a fig. That is twice this week.
Warm stone, cool breeze. Somebody planned this town well.
Mange takk, everyone. For nothing in particular.
I complimented Théo's bread. He bowed. Deeply.
A good afternoon is mostly shade and people saying hei.
Pink flowers over every doorway. They have outdone themselves.
Just standing here. It is allowed. I asked Odile.
Marcel's terrace is full of hats. Good afternoon for hats.
Somebody's laundry is drying in the breeze. Very cheerful socks.
Léo is teaching the fountain a new trick. It is mostly splashing.
Three kids, one pigeon, zero urgency. A good afternoon.
The fountain sounds different at four. Lazier, somehow.
Someone drew a hopscotch by the kiosk. I did it. Quietly.
Afternoon. The shadows have moved one café table to the left.
Henri's lemons are glowing. Not literally. Almost.
Odile told me the time without looking at a clock. She was right.
Four o'clock. The town leans back in its chair.
Léo floated a leaf in the fountain. It has a crew of one ant.
Hei. You found the slow part of the day.
If you stand here long enough, someone offers you a grape.
Camille just stopped to smell a geranium. Then a second one.
Théo hums the same four notes every afternoon. I like them.
The cypresses are casting stripes on the street. Free zebra.
The café awning is half down. That means it is properly afternoon.
Takk, afternoon. You are very easy to like.
A kite went up behind the houses. Somebody is having a great day.
Children racing the pigeons. The pigeons are winning, politely.
I keep a list of good moments. This one goes on it.
Every window on this street has a flowerpot. I counted.
Afternoon light makes the zinc roofs look silver. Nydelig.
A grandmother just won at hopscotch. Huge applause.
I am not doing much right now. That is the whole plan.
The kids have invented a game. The rules change every minute.
Afternoon tea at home is good. Afternoon tea here is better.
The fountain has a little rainbow at this hour. Look low.
Henri's watering can is older than me. It still pours true.
The palms are rustling like a polite audience.
Every lamp post here has a name. I am still learning them.
The tower house window catches the sun at this hour. Mine.
Léo just explained gravity to me. Mostly correct.
Walking slowly. The sea is not in a hurry either.
The promenade has exactly the right number of benches.
Every lap someone waves. Today it was a toddler. Big wave.
Hands in pockets, nowhere to be. Lovely.
Halfway round. The cypress at the corner says hello.
The kids have chalked a racetrack. I am walking the slow lane.
I walk past the fountain twice a lap. Once is never enough.
Odile waved from the bench. I bowed. She laughed.
Promenade, fountain, café, repeat. A fine little circuit.
Walking past the windows, guessing which lamp lights first.
My thoughts untangle about one bench at a time.
Léo's sandcastle has a moat now. Real engineering.
Walking makes the afternoon last longer. I have tested it.
The pavement is warm. The air is warm. The whole town is warm.
One more lap. The light is too good to go in.
I pass Henri's lemons and say hei. Habit by now.
The kids are skipping. I am walking in rhythm. Do not tell.
The builder has a new pencil behind his ear. A good sign.
Through the glass: one radio, two mugs, plenty of focus.
I knock. He points at the kettle. Good answer.
Kids pressing noses to the workshop glass. He waves at them.
The workshop lamp is not on yet. Too much sun for it.
We talked for ten minutes and solved one small thing. Nice.
The builder is whistling. That is my favourite progress report.
Shavings curl on the floor like little ribbons.
The radio is playing jazz. The saw keeps time.
Kiosk coffee in the afternoon. A tiny celebration.
A paper cup and a view. That is the whole order.
The kiosk sells lemonade now. Henri approves.
The kiosk radio and the café radio are playing the same song.
Coffee with a view of children and pigeons. Five stars.
Leaning on the kiosk counter. Very continental of me.
Afternoon coffee tastes like the evening is coming.
A small coffee. A big sky. Takk.
Léo bought a lollipop with three coins and a speech.
From the kiosk you can see three lamp posts. Waiting their turn.
Here is the secret of the kiosk: nobody is ever in a hurry.
Hei hei. Afternoon already. Where did lunch go?
Somewhere a radio is playing accordion. Very on brand.
Hello, gull. You again. Same post, same opinion.
Why do afternoons here feel twice as long? In a good way.
The fountain sounds louder after lunch. Or I listen better.
I wonder who planted the first cypress. Good call, whoever.
Cicadas. Up north we would call this a concert.
Afternoon, Henri. The watering can is winning again.
Is it the bakery or the café? The whole street smells of butter.
A bicycle bell, two streets away. Lucie, probably.
Hei, Léo. Faster than yesterday? Looked like it.
How does Odile know everyone's birthday? I should ask her.
Somebody is frying garlic. Somebody is a hero.
God ettermiddag. That is afternoon, more or less.
Bonjour to the shutters. Half of them are napping.
Hei, Théo. Is that a second baguette? Respect.
Smells like jasmine on this corner. Every single day.
I keep counting zinc roofs. I lose count at the café.
That is the sound of Marcel laughing. From the far terrace.
Who chose the blue for the café shutters? Perfect blue.
Afternoon, Camille. Léo told me about the lamps theory.
Hello there. Lost? Everyone is, a little. It is nice.
Sun on my face, sea in my ears. Fine office.
There is a bee in the rosemary that works harder than me.
Hei. You look like someone who just found the kiosk.
Where do the gulls go at three? Same place every day, I bet.
The promenade tiles click under every shoe. I like that.
Hei, Henri. Still on the bench? Still the best bench.
Strolling speed. The town insists on it after lunch.
Sea breeze on this stretch. Salt and sun cream.
Bonjour, madame. Yes, the fountain is always this happy.
I wonder what Odile and Henri talk about. Everything, I think.
Halfway down the promenade the café smell takes over.
Afternoon, Léo! Who is winning? Both of you? Good.
That lamp post always hums a little. A friendly hum.
Hei, Camille. Wandering too? It is the afternoon thing.
Is it rude to stroll faster than Henri? I slow down anyway.
The string lights tick in the breeze. Waiting for evening.
Here it smells of figs. Which house has the fig tree?
Hei, little one. Yes, you can race me. I will lose.
The fountain, the bell, the gulls. Afternoon soundtrack.
Long shadows starting. The cypresses are getting tall.
Good afternoon, neighbour. Lovely hat. New?
Pétanque somewhere. That little clack. Very satisfying.
Does the sea sound different in the afternoon? Softer?
Théo is pretending to work on the bench. Good form.
Warm bread and cool sea. That is the whole promenade.
Wonder how many steps one lap is. Inès would know.
The fountain coins sparkle at this hour. Lots of wishes.
That whirr is the drill. That hum is the builder.
Afternoon. I brought nothing but questions.
The window glass is warm. The sun has been watching too.
He measures twice. I counted. Then once more, for luck.
Pencil shavings and varnish. Smells like progress.
Tap tap, little hammer. Someone is in a good mood.
Hello in there. I will just watch. I am good at watching.
I wonder how many mugs live in that workshop. Six? Ten?
Nice and tidy in there today. Did the broom get a raise?
One wave through the window, one wave back. Our ritual.
Does the workbench have a name? It feels like it should.
Hei! One coffee, please. The usual, if I have one.
Fresh coffee and newspaper ink. The kiosk smell.
What is the pastry of the day? I trust you completely.
The cup is warm. The bench is near. Excellent planning.
Is that cardamom? Somebody here knows the north.
Afternoon coffee, outside, in the sun. Small victory.
Lucie said order the small one and a biscuit. Obviously.
The milk frother sounds like a tiny happy dragon.
Hello, queue. We are all in no hurry. Wonderful.
Takk. Merci. Thank you. I like to cover all options.
How many postcards on this rack? I count a whole summer.
Coffee in one hand, sun in the other. Balanced.
The kiosk bell does a little ding. Everyone looks happy.
Orange peel and espresso. Who thought of that? Genius.
Hei, neighbour. Coffee? It is that time again.
Is the striped awning new? It was always new, I think.
First sip. The rest of the afternoon is officially on.
That sugar packet has a little cypress on it. Cute.
Practising my French Rs on the cat. She is unimpressed but patient.
Day twelve of learning to whistle with two fingers. Some air came out.
Henri is teaching me chess. I know how the horse moves. Mostly.
My first day here, Odile gave me directions and a peach. I kept both.
I can now count to vingt without stopping. Next week: trente.
Learning to sketch cypresses. Mine look like confident carrots.
Trying to tie a scarf the way Odile does. It became a small knot.
The first time I heard the café radio, I stayed for three songs.
Practising patience. The fig on Henri's tree is nearly ready.
I am learning the names of the flowers. That one is bougainvillea.
Léo taught me a card trick. I know the trick. Not the card.
Watercolours today. The sea came out lovely. The sky came out sea.
The day I moved in, the whole street helped carry one sofa. Laughing.
Juggling practice: two lemons, yes. Three lemons, Henri is watching.
My accent is improving. Marcel only smiled a little bit this time.
I still remember my first croissant here. Flaky, and all over me.
Learning to say bonne après-midi without it sounding like a sneeze.
Henri showed me how to read the weather in the cypresses. Fine today.
Practising my hopscotch. The kids say my form is very Norwegian.
The year it rained on the festival, everyone just danced under it.
I can now carry two coffees and a croissant. A real skill.
Learning the town's songs. I know the chorus to two. Proudly.
Camille taught me to tell ripe figs by touch. Gentle squeeze.
This bench is where I first met Henri. He offered half the shade.
Ukulele, week three. Two chords and a lot of enthusiasm.
Today's lesson from Léo: snails are not slow, they are thorough.
I remember when they hung the first string lights. Whole town cheered.
Trying to learn which bell is the church and which is Lucie.
Memorising a French poem. Four lines in. Odile mouths along.
Théo is coaching my baguette selection. Firm crust, good sound.
Learning to cook ratatouille. Marcel says less rushing, more love.
First summer here I got so sunburnt Odile called me her tomato.
Henri says I water too fast. Lesson two: let the soil drink.
Writing a little in my notebook. Today: the colour of four o'clock.
Léo and I are learning to skip stones. Me: three. Him: five.
Odile once taught me a waltz right here. The fountain kept time.
Practising my wave. Not too big, not too small. The town wave.
Learning bird calls. That one is a gull. I am very sure of that one.
Henri taught me to peel an orange in one long ribbon. Nearly.
My first afternoon here, I sat on that wall for two hours. Smiling.
Learning to enjoy coffee without a laptop. Day three. Going well.
Lucie is teaching me to ride with no hands. In theory, so far.
I can name every shop on this street. Mostly by smell.
The day Léo lost his first tooth, he showed the entire promenade.
Camille taught me a paper bird. Mine looks like a happy envelope.
Remember the picnic on the steps? Théo brought six cheeses.
Knitting lesson with Odile tomorrow. I have bought blue wool.
Learning the slow walk. Henri has mastered it. I am an apprentice.
Last spring the whole town painted shutters together. Mine is green.
I am getting better at pétanque. I hit the little ball once. Once!
Learning to nap in the afternoon. A very French skill. Hard work.
Learning to plane wood. The shavings get longer every week.
He taught me the right way to hold a hammer. I hold it so well now.
My first try at a dovetail joint. More of a dove-ish joint.
I remember the day he opened these doors. One lamp and a big grin.
Practising my knots on his bench. Square knot. Mostly square.
He is teaching me to sand with the grain. Calm work. I like it.
The first thing I built in here was a stool. It still stands. Just.
Lesson today: measure, pencil, breathe, then cut. Good lesson.
Learning the names of his tools. That is a spokeshave. Lovely word.
Remember when the kids painted his sign? Every letter a new colour.
Practising sharpening a chisel. He says listen to the stone.
He let me drill a hole today. Straight! He gave a small hum.
My little birdhouse from last summer still hangs by his door.
Learning to read his diagrams. The squiggle is a spring. I think.
Practising my bonjour on every bench. Henri gave it a seven.
This is the stretch where Léo learned to ride. We all clapped.
Learning to walk without looking at my feet. The view is better.
I remember my first lap of this promenade. I got lost. On a line.
Counting palms in French as I go. Quatorze. I think there are more.
Odile taught me to tip an imaginary hat. I do it all the time now.
That bench is where Henri and I watched the summer stars. Lovely.
Practising walking and whistling at once. Walking is going fine.
Here is where Biscuit first decided I was a friend. Big day.
I am learning every house colour. That one is apricot, not orange.
Last winter it snowed for ten minutes. Everyone ran out right here.
Camille is teaching me the names of the herbs along here. Thyme.
This corner is where I learned the word flâner. To stroll, happily.
Practising my French on the shop signs. Boulangerie. Nailed it.
I remember carrying Léo's kite all the way down here. It flew!
Every lap I learn one new thing. Today: the fountain has a fish on it.
Here is where Marcel taught me to say merci like I mean it.
Ordering in French today. Un petit café. She did not even blink.
My first order here was a hot chocolate. In July. She still laughs.
Learning to drink espresso in one go. Like a local. Almost.
The kiosk lady is teaching me one word a day. Today: délicieux.
Practising the crossword here. I got one across all by myself.
I remember sharing a whole bag of biscuits here with Léo. In the rain.
Learning the coin names. This small gold one buys me a biscuit.
Lucie taught me to dunk a biscuit for exactly three seconds.
Today I ordered without pointing. A big moment for me.
This corner of the kiosk is where Henri first called me neighbour.
Learning to read the kiosk paper. I understood the weather. Sunny.
Henri, does the lemon bench get the morning sun or the evening?
One shutter on the yellow house is open exactly halfway. Every day.
Odile, is that a new brooch? It looks like a tiny lemon.
Somebody chalked a smiley on the fountain step. Still there.
Marcel folds napkins into little fans after lunch. Forty, at least.
The tower clock is two minutes behind the café clock. Both fine.
A geranium is growing out of a teapot on that balcony.
A single red balloon is tied to the café railing. Somebody's birthday.
Léo, why only the white tiles? Ah. Rules. Of course.
The fountain splashes higher on the left. I have no explanation.
A palm shadow is touching the tip of my shoe. Hello, palm.
The bakery sign says back at four, in very curly letters.
Thyme or oregano in that window box? Henri would know.
One lamp post has a little dent. Like a dimple.
Marcel, do you ever sit on your own terrace? Just once?
Every café chair faces the sea. Except one. That one faces Odile.
Somebody hung a wind chime made of old spoons. It works.
Odile, how do you always know which bench is in the shade?
The postbox is a slightly different red on one side. Charming.
Lucie has tied a sprig of lavender to her bike basket today.
Henri waters the pots in the same order. Left, right, lemon.
Is it just me, or does the fountain take a breath before four?
Two neighbours are passing a cake across the street. Window to window.
There is a nest near the top of that cypress. Busy tenants.
Camille, has Léo named the pigeons yet? He hinted he would.
The breeze flipped a café menu to the desserts. Taking the hint.
One tile on the square is shaped like a heart. Find it.
Bonjour, lavender. Hei, rosemary. I greet the herbs now.
Afternoon. My shadow is finally taller than me again.
Marcel, is it tarte day or clafoutis day? I am ready for both.
A butterfly is taking the same route as me. Two regulars.
Someone upstairs is ironing by the open window. Very neat shirts.
Did you notice the fountain has four faces? One is smiling.
The corner house shutters are three different greens. All good.
How many coffees has that kettle made today? Roughly?
He keeps one drawer just for things that might be useful.
A tiny spirit level on the windowsill. The sill is level. Of course.
Is that a new apron? It has a pocket for every pencil.
He sharpens pencils with a knife. Neat little curls.
What are the offcuts for? A bird box, he says.
A sticky note on the window says nearly. I like nearly.
The visitor stool has my name on it in chalk now.
Which tool do you reach for first? He held up a pencil.
A jar of buttons on the shelf. Nobody knows why. Nobody minds.
There is a plant on the workbench. He waters it between screws.
The sun reaches the vise at four. He calls it vise o'clock.
Do the drawers have names? He pointed. They have names.
One fingerprint on the window. Mine, from yesterday.
He offered me a biscuit from the washer tin. Wrong tin. We laughed.
A sawhorse wearing his jacket. Very relaxed sawhorse.
Can I pass you anything? He said: your opinion. Kind.
A fresh drawing on the wall. Lots of arrows, all pointing up.
He tests every chair leg twice. The wobbly one, three times.
His mug says Monday. It is not Monday. Still a cheerful mug.
Henri, which way are you walking? Same as me? Lovely.
Every third tile on this stretch is a little pinker.
The benches have little name plaques. I read one per lap.
Someone tied ribbons on the railing. Yellow, blue, yellow.
Odile, a shortcut to the café? No, she says. That is the point.
A lizard on the warm wall. One push-up, then off he goes.
My steps match the fountain drips for about ten metres.
The rosemary hedge brushed my sleeve. Now I smell like dinner.
Lucie, does your bell have a name? It sounds like it does.
One palm has two old initials in a little heart.
A tiny sun hat hung on the railing for its owner. Kind town.
The string lights cast a lace pattern on the tiles.
Léo, how do you dance and walk at the same time? Teach me.
One shop door has a bell with two notes. Ding-dong, very polite.
Round the fountain clockwise today. Feels brand new.
Is that Camille laughing? It carries a whole block.
The breeze handed me one petal. It is in my pocket now.
Bakery chalkboard: pain aux raisins. Noted for later.
A street musician bowed to me. I bowed back. Mutual respect.
Henri's hat is tilted east today. Means he is in fine spirits.
A coin in the fountain basin has a little sun on it.
A dog I have never met just sat on my foot. Bonjour to you too.
Théo, which bench is yours today? You seem to rotate.
